title: Live Median House Price
story: A local news site has a housing page with one headline number: the median sale price in town this year. The median, not the average, because one mansion selling for millions would drag the average far above what a typical home costs.

Sales are reported one at a time as they close, and the page shows the updated median right away. By the end of the year there are thousands of sales, and recomputing from scratch every time makes the page slow.
task:
• constructor(): no sales yet.
  • addSale(price): record one sale.
  • median(): return the median of all prices recorded so far. With an odd number of sales it is the middle price once they are sorted; with an even number it is the average of the two middle prices (which may end in .5). With no sales, return null (None in Python).
addSale should take O(log n) time and median O(1), where n is the number of sales so far.
constraints: Every median is a whole number or ends in .5, so answers are compared exactly.

examples.explanation: One sale: 300000. Two sales, 250000 and 300000: the average of the two is 275000. Add the 2,000,000 mansion: the sorted prices are 250000, 300000, 2000000, so the median is 300000; the mansion barely moves it. Add 280000: the middle two are 280000 and 300000, median 290000.
Before any sale there is no median: null. After 5 and 6 the median is 5.5, so the answer is not always a whole number.

hints: Suppose the sorted prices are split into a lower half and an upper half. To read the median, which prices do you actually need to see? Do you need the rest of each half in order?
You only need the largest price of the lower half and the smallest price of the upper half. Everything else in each half can stay unordered.

A max-heap keeps the largest of the lower half on top; a min-heap keeps the smallest of the upper half on top. When a new sale arrives, how do you put it in the right half, and how do you stop the halves from drifting apart in size?

Keep low (a max-heap) and high (a min-heap) with low holding the same number of prices as high or one more. To add: push onto low, move low's top to high, and if high is now bigger, move high's top back. The median is low's top for an odd count, or the average of both tops for an even count.
bruteForce: Keep all prices in a list and sort it every time median() is called. That costs O(n log n) per call, so a year of 25,000 sales with a median after each is about 4 billion steps.

Keeping the list sorted by inserting each price in its place (binary search for the spot) is better, but inserting into the middle of an array still shifts up to n elements, so it is O(n) per sale and O(n²) for the year.

js: /** @return {number|null} median of all sales so far */

tests.note: largest prices; the average is not a whole number
defeats taking the middle of the arrival order without sorting
new sales land below, above, then below the middle: each must reach the right half

js: this.low = new Heap((a, b) => a > b);  // max-heap: lower half
this.high = new Heap((a, b) => a < b); // min-heap: upper half
this.high.push(this.low.pop()); // the largest of low may belong in high

const a = this.a, top = a[0], last = a.pop();
if (l < a.length && this.before(a[l], a[m])) m = l;
if (r < a.length && this.before(a[r], a[m])) m = r;

self.high = []  # upper half as a min-heap

walkthrough: The median only depends on the one or two prices in the middle. Split the sales into a lower half and an upper half. Keep the lower half in a max-heap so its largest price is on top, and the upper half in a min-heap so its smallest price is on top. Those two tops sit right at the middle.

Two rules keep it correct: every price in low is ≤ every price in high, and low has the same size as high or one more. Pushing into low and then passing low's top to high keeps the first rule; moving one back when high gets too big keeps the second.
• add 300: low {300} → pass 300 to high → high is bigger, move it back. low {300}, high {}. Median 300.
• add 250: low {300, 250} → pass the top, 300, to high. low {250}, high {300}. Sizes equal. Median (250 + 300) / 2 = 275.
• add 2000: low {2000, 250} → pass 2000 to high. high {300, 2000} is bigger, so move 300 back. low {300, 250}, high {2000}. Median 300.
Step 3 shows why the price goes through low first: the mansion landed in the upper half, where it belongs, and could not pull the median up.
solution.timeWhy: addSale does at most three heap pushes or pops; median only reads the two tops, which is O(1).
solution.spaceWhy: Every price is stored in one of the two heaps.
solution.takeaway: To track a middle value of a changing collection, split it into two heaps that face each other: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, kept balanced in size. The same two-heap idea answers any running percentile.
